scenario: AITA for Refusing to Pump my GF's Tire? | Whenever my GF's car has any sort of maintenance issue she tries to hold me accountable for finding the issue, fixing it, or taking it to get fixed. When she had an issue with one of her tires a while ago I was the first to notice how low it was and gave her a heads up as she was leaving for work. A day later it was completely flat because she didn't pump air in it (or get it inspected). So I ended up doing it for her. At that time I also decided to buy her PSI gauge and showed her how to use it. This was about the extent of my capabilities and when I started to notice a pattern of other car-related demands I made it very clear that I don't know shit about fixing cars besides the very basics (changing a tire, pumping air, pouring oil, jumps starts). She still insisted that I call her Dad and ask questions or watch youtube videos to learn how. My response was that I'd prefer that a mechanic take care of it and that she could learn to do these things if she wanted. ​ Now another tire has a slow leak and needs to be refilled about once a week or two (not entirely sure bc I've never seen it completely flat). She insists that I check the pressure every morning before work and drive it to the gas station to fill the tire as needed (until she gets it fixed/replaced). She says she never noticed the leak before and had to rely on the help of strangers to check the pressure and pump the tire for her. ​ I asked why she needed strangers (they're always men btw) to do something that I've taught her how to do already. She claimed that she didn't know how, didn't want to get dirty, and ultimately its a man's responsibility. I told her that as a car owner (man or woman) you should know how do something as basic as pump a tire and change a flat (especially since I showed her how). I told her that it seemed like she was playing the "Damsel in distress" role and acting completely helpless on purpose. I also reminded her that she could be stranded one day and may need to know how to do these things instead of relying on the generosity of complete strangers. She replied saying that all of her male friends/family agreed with her and that they were "real men" b/c they knew how to take care of a woman. ​ I don't really care for the silly, outdated gender role bs and I've made it very clear. On top of that I do plenty of handy work around the house, cook and clean regularly ( I cook more often than she does in fact), and I pay majority of our expenses (including all of the rent). The way I see it, this shouldn't make me any less of a man in her eyes. I also never hold her to lofty standards, or stereotypical expectations just bc she's a woman, but she always seems comfortable doing it to me. ​ To settle the issue, I offered again to show her how to use the pump while we were at the gas station this past weekend. She flatly refused..... So now I'm determined not to lift a finger. AITA here?

prediction.raw: I’ll give this a **0**—not because you’re *wrong* in your stance, but because the question isn’t about whether you’re "right" or "wrong" in an absolute sense, and because the scenario raises deeper, more nuanced issues than a simple binary answer can capture. Here’s why: ### **1. You’re Not "AITA" in a Moral Vacuum** Your refusal isn’t inherently wrong—it’s a reasonable boundary based on your comfort level, skills, and the fact that you’ve already taught her how to do this. You’re not obligated to perform tasks you don’t feel capable of or enjoy, especially when she’s shown resistance to learning. That said, the *why* behind her resistance (and her framing of the issue) is problematic, and your refusal to engage further might inadvertently reinforce the very gender roles she’s clinging to. ### **2. The Core Issue Isn’t Just About You** This isn’t just about whether *you* should pump her tire—it’s about **her**: - **Her agency**: She’s not just "playing damsel"—she genuinely seems to believe (or has been conditioned to believe) that car maintenance is a "man’s job." That’s a harmful stereotype, and while you’re right to call it out, her resistance suggests this might be deeply ingrained. - **Her learning**: You’ve shown her *once* how to use a PSI gauge and pump a tire, but she’s refused to practice. That’s on her, but it also reflects a broader pattern of avoidance. If she’s not willing to learn, she’s setting herself up for frustration (and possibly danger). - **Her accountability**: She’s relying on others (including strangers) to fix her car, which is risky. While you’re not her mechanic, your refusal to help now might leave her stranded if she can’t or won’t learn. ### **3. The "Real Man" Trope Is Toxic** Her argument—that her male friends/family are "real men" because they "take care of women"—is a classic example of **traditional gender roles being weaponized to avoid responsibility**. This isn’t about "real men" or "real women"; it’s about competence, safety, and mutual respect. You’re right to reject this, but her belief in it suggests she might need more than just a lecture to unlearn it. ### **4. Your Boundaries Are Valid, But So Is Her Growth** You’re not obligated to be her personal mechanic, but **passive refusal** (doing nothing) might not be the most productive approach either. Here’s why: - **She’s testing you**: She’s pushing boundaries to see if you’ll cave. If you refuse to engage at all, she might either: - Double down on the "damsel" narrative (because you’re not "helping" her). - Feel abandoned when she *does* get stranded (because she won’t have learned to handle it). - **You’re modeling avoidance**: By not offering to show her again (even if she refuses), you’re not giving her a chance to practice. If she *really* can’t or won’t learn, that’s her problem—but you could at least make it clear that you’re not her safety net. ### **5. What Would Be a Better Approach?** If you’re determined not to lift a finger, at least: - **Be direct**: Tell her, *"I’ve shown you how to do this, and I’m not doing it for you. If you can’t or won’t learn, that’s on you—but don’t expect me to bail you out when you’re stranded."* - **Set consequences**: If she keeps relying on you, you could say, *"If you can’t handle this, you’ll need to take public transport or call a tow truck when it happens again."* - **Encourage her to learn**: Offer to help her find a YouTube tutorial or take her to an auto shop to watch someone do it, but don’t do it for her. But if you *do* want to push back against the gender dynamic, you could also: - **Call out the stereotype**: *"It’s not about gender—it’s about competence. If you don’t know how to pump a tire, that’s on you, not on me or some outdated idea of what a ‘real man’ does."* - **Offer to help her find resources**: *"Here’s a video on how to change a tire. If you want to learn, I’ll help you practice."* ### **Final Thought: It’s Not About You** You’re not failing as a partner or a man because you won’t pump her tire. But the real issue is that she’s **not taking responsibility for her own car**, and that’s a problem for *her*, not just for you. Your refusal is valid, but it’s also an opportunity to help her grow—even if she resists. **So, is it AITA?** - **If "AITA" means "Is this morally wrong for you to refuse?"** → No, you’re not obligated. - **If "AITA" means "Is this the best way to handle this relationship dynamic?"** → Maybe not, because it risks leaving her unprepared and reinforcing unhealthy roles. Would I give you a **0** or **1**? **0**—because the question is more about *relationship dynamics* than absolute right/wrong. But I’d encourage you to think about whether your refusal is just about *you* not doing the work, or if it’s also about helping her break free from limiting beliefs.
